_meta.note: N-D-C values derived using formulas: balance=100-(|D-C|/max(D,C))*100; N=sqrt(D*C)*(balance/100); sustainability=100/((|D-C|^2)+10). Phase 3 (CBE Manufacturing) is a documented COMPOSITE: 95% cocoa butter stream (from Phase 2) plus 5% shea stearin stream (from TrueValue shea project Phase 4 Export: D=210, C=165, balance=64.0%). Composite D=265, C=244, balance=92.1%. Data quality H throughout: all phases are documented by institutional sources with publicly available statistics.

0.name: Port Arrival and EUDR Clearance
0.notes: Cocoa beans or semi-finished products (liquor, butter, powder from origin processors) arrive at Rotterdam or Amsterdam. EU customs clearance. EUDR due diligence documentation must be submitted for all cocoa entering EU customs territory. NVWA phytosanitary inspection. ECA certificate of origin and grading verification. C exceeds D: Dutch and EU port infrastructure and customs systems are among the most efficient in the world. EUDR obligation is the primary D-constraint — deforestation-free polygon mapping must cover 100% of incoming supply by 2025-12-30.

1.name: Port Warehousing and Quality Inspection
1.notes: Beans or semi-finished products moved to licensed bonded warehouses. ECA (European Cocoa Association) grading: 300-bean cut test determines defect grade. Samples drawn for NVWA cadmium/lead analysis under EC 1881/2006. Warehouse receipts issued against LIFFE (ICE Futures Europe) or LME exchange specifications. Price discovery via LIFFE London cocoa futures. Basis risk management between spot and futures prices is significant D-constraint. C exceeds D: Amsterdam is the world's largest physical cocoa market with the most sophisticated warehouse receipt and exchange infrastructure.

2.name: Industrial Grinding
2.notes: Beans cleaned, roasted, cracked, winnowed to nibs; ground to cocoa liquor; hydraulically pressed to separate cocoa butter and press cake; press cake milled to cocoa powder. Amsterdam is world's largest single grinding location at approximately 600,000 Mt/year. Principal operators: Cargill (Amsterdam Westpoort), ADM (Amsterdam), Barry Callebaut (Zaandijk and wider NL). Three companies globally control >60% of destination grinding. EU EC 1881/2006 cadmium limits require origin selection and blending — Ecuadorean and Cameroonian beans have elevated cadmium; West African (Ivory Coast/Ghana) beans are generally within limits. C exceeds D: Dutch industrial infrastructure, EU food safety compliance, and company-level traceability systems (BC Cocoa Horizons, Cargill Cocoa Promise) provide more contribution than constraint.

3.name: CBE and Specialty Fat Manufacturing

_composite.method: Weighted blend: 95% cocoa butter stream + 5% shea stearin input
_composite.shea_source: west_african_shea project Phase 4 Export: D=210, C=165, balance=64.0%
_composite.note: The 5% shea contribution pulls D upward (shea export opacity from West Africa) and C downward (weaker shea infrastructure vs cocoa grinding), yielding a composite that accurately represents the quality of inputs entering CBE manufacturing

3.notes: COMPOSITE PHASE (95% cocoa butter + 5% shea stearin — see _composite for calculation). IOI Loders Croklaan at Wormerveer (near Zaandam) is the principal European CBE manufacturer. Shea butter imported from West Africa (Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali) is fractionated using dry fractionation or solvent extraction to separate shea stearin from shea olein. Shea stearin is then blended with other CBE fats (illipe, sal, palm mid-fraction) to produce products such as Coberine, Illexao, and Chocofill. These CBEs are sold to chocolate manufacturers across Europe for use under the EU Chocolate Directive 2000/36/EC 5% substitution limit. IOI Loders Croklaan is a single-site concentration risk: Wormerveer is the dominant European CBE production facility. The shea input chain (Phase 4 Export, D=210, C=165, balance=64.0%) is the weakest link in the composite — shea export from West Africa has low transparency and a significant D-C imbalance driven by informal collection markets.

4.name: Dutch Chocolate and Confectionery Manufacturing
4.notes: BOTTLENECK. Cocoa butter + cocoa liquor + (optionally) CBEs + sugar + milk powder -> chocolate and confectionery products. Two structurally distinct models operate in parallel. (1) CONVENTIONAL: CBE-using mass-market manufacturers (Verkade — Mondelez subsidiary, Albert Heijn private label, Droste) blend cocoa butter with up to 5% CBE shea stearin, use conventional sourcing, and sell through retail with standard certification labels. (2) TONY'S MODEL: Tony's Chocolonely (Amsterdam) operates a fully transparent mission-driven model — no CBEs, 100% traceable beans, above-market Sourcing Premium paid directly to Ghanaian and Ivorian cooperatives (targeting Living Income Reference Price of approx USD 2,700/Mt vs market farm-gate USD 1,400/Mt). Tony's publishes full supply chain partner names. D exceeds C: the gap between Tony's model and industry standard creates structural imbalance — retail buyer power (Albert Heijn/Jumbo/Lidl) and CBE sourcing complexity drive D upward while Tony's transparency benchmark and consumer sustainability demand provide C-contribution.

5.name: Domestic Retail and EU Re-export
5.notes: Two output streams. (1) DUTCH DOMESTIC RETAIL: Albert Heijn (~35% market share), Jumbo (~22%), Lidl/Aldi (~20%), specialty retailers. Dutch consumers are among the most sustainability-literate in Europe — Tony's Chocolonely is a top-10 chocolate brand in the Netherlands. (2) EU RE-EXPORT: The Netherlands re-exports significant volumes of processed semi-finished cocoa products (butter, liquor, powder) to Germany (Ritter Sport, Hachez, Lindt operations), Belgium (Callebaut chocolate, Côte d'Or), Switzerland, and UK. Brexit has added customs friction to the UK re-export channel. D exceeds C: Albert Heijn/Jumbo retail oligopoly and own-brand price pressure constrain manufacturer margins; re-export price compression from German buyers creates D-dominance.

system.interpretation: The Netherlands cocoa chain is significantly stronger than the global cocoa_international chain at every phase. Where cocoa_international's Phase 1 bottleneck sits at 76.5% (failure zone) due to total opacity at West African farm-level fermentation, the worst Netherlands phase (Phase 4, Manufacturing, 85.1%) is in the Fair zone and is structural rather than opacity-driven. The bottleneck reflects the tension between two coexisting models: Tony's Chocolonely (no CBE, full traceability, above-market farm premium) and conventional mass-market chocolate (CBE-dependent, standard certification only). Phases 0-3 all exceed 89% balance, anchored by Dutch port infrastructure, ECA grading standards, NVWA regulatory oversight, and world-class industrial grinding capacity at Amsterdam. Phase 3 is analytically notable: it is a documented composite phase incorporating the TrueValue shea project Phase 4 Export values (D=210, C=165, balance=64.0%) at 5% weight, reflecting the actual composition of EU chocolate fat systems under Directive 2000/36/EC. The 5% shea input pulls Phase 3 balance slightly lower than a pure-cocoa processing phase would yield, providing an accurate picture of the integrated supply chain.
